entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Henry of Blois (c. 1100 – 8 July 1171), grandson of William the Conqueror and younger brother of King Stephen, was a powerful and controversial figure in 12th-century England. As Abbot of Glastonbury from 1126 and Bishop of Winchester from 1129, he wielded immense ecclesiastical and political influence during the tumultuous period known as The Anarchy (1135–1153). His career exemplifies the intricate entanglement of church and state, aristocratic ambition, and the flourishing of Romanesque and early Gothic architecture in high medieval Europe, particularly within the Anglo-Norman realm.

Educated at Cluny Abbey, Henry brought sophisticated monastic ideals and administrative acumen to England. He transformed Glastonbury Abbey into one of England's wealthiest and most influential monastic houses, initiating extensive building programs and acquiring numerous relics. As Bishop of Winchester, he fortified his episcopal residences, including Wolvesey Castle, and played a crucial, often shifting, role in the civil war between his brother Stephen and Empress Matilda. He initially supported Stephen but later briefly sided with Matilda, even proclaiming her 'Lady of the English' in 1141, before returning to Stephen's cause. His vast wealth, derived from his ecclesiastical holdings and personal estates, allowed him to maintain private armies and exert significant leverage over both secular and spiritual affairs, effectively acting as a kingmaker.
